1.pericope_label: In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah began Hoshea the son of Elah to reign in Samaria over Israel nine years. And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, but not as the kings of Israel that were before him. Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria; and Hoshea became his servant, and gave him presents. And the king of Assyria found conspiracy in Hoshea: for he had sent messengers to So king of Egypt, and brought no present to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year: therefore the king of Assyria shut him up, and bound him in prison. Then the king of Assyria came up throughout all the land, and went up to Samaria, and besieged it three years. In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.

schools.summary: Ellicott recomputes the accession, arguing that if Pekah reigned thirty years and Ahaz succeeded in his seventeenth, then Ahaz reigned thirteen years concurrently with Pekah and Hoshea came in during his fourteenth; he cites the inscription of Tiglath Pileser to show Hoshea was an Assyrian vassal from the start, doubts that he abandoned the Bethel worship, keeps Shalmaneser the Fourth distinct from Sargon, and observes that the narrative never says Shalmaneser besieged Samaria three years and took it, since Sargon claims the capture in his own first year. On the Egyptian alliance he points the name Sewe, identifies him with Shabaka whom Sargon beat at Raphia, and notes that Sargon calls him a prince rather than a king. Keil and Delitzsch identify Shalmaneser with the Sargon of Isaiah, whose name is spelt Sargina on the monuments, take So for one of the two Shebeks of the Ethiopian dynasty without settling which, and insist that the places of exile lie in provinces of Assyria and Media rather than in Mesopotamia.

Gill meets the chronological difficulty with an interregnum, or else with the supposition that Hoshea was not generally acknowledged as king until the twelfth year of Ahaz. He takes Shalmaneser for the son and successor of Tiglath-pileser, citing the Tyrian archives that Josephus reports and a chronicler who gives him seventeen years, and notes of the calves that Hoshea could not have worshipped them since one had already been carried away.

Clarke also makes Shalmaneser the son and successor of Tiglath-pileser, adding that Hosea calls him Shalman and the book of Tobit Enemessar; he says a city holding out three years must have been well fortified and provisioned, cites Hosea and Micah for the cruelties done when it fell, and argues at length after Sir William Jones that the Afghans are descended from the captive tribes. Wesley says Hoshea usurped the kingdom in the fourth year of Ahaz but was not established until the twelfth, notes that the older Hebrew writers identified Shalmaneser with Sennacherib since one man in the East may carry several names, and closes on the disappearance of the tribes, that they who forgot God were themselves forgotten.

Henry reads the delay before the throne as a chastisement and finds the word of Hosea fulfilled in it, now they shall say, We have no king. He presses the difficulty that the ruin came under one of the better kings, and answers that God was reckoning the iniquities of foregoing ages and the sins of a people whose king gave them leave to do better; on the revolt he calls Egypt a broken reed and says that men get nothing by struggling with the net but entangle themselves the more.

7.pericope_label: For so it was, that the children of Israel had sinned against the Lord their God, which had brought them up out of the land of Egypt, from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and had feared other gods, And walked in the statutes of the heathen, whom the Lord cast out from before the children of Israel, and of the kings of Israel, which they had made. And the children of Israel did secretly those things that were not right against the Lord their God, and they built them high places in all their cities, from the tower of the watchmen to the fenced city. And they set them up images and groves in every high hill, and under every green tree: And there they burnt incense in all the high places, as did the heathen whom the Lord carried away before them; and wrought wicked things to provoke the Lord to anger: For they served idols, whereof the Lord had said unto them, Ye shall not do this thing.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the opening words as and it came to pass when rather than because, so that the sentence does not close until the eighteenth verse and everything between is explanation; they find the apostasy running in two directions, the statutes of the nations and the statutes the kings of Israel had made, and follow Hengstenberg in taking the disputed clause of covering words that were not right concerning Jehovah, an attempt to conceal the nature of the revealed God by perversions of his word, rejecting both the rendering that they trifled with such things and the rendering that they dealt perfidiously. On the last verse they render the word the clods, masses of stone worshipped as gods. Ellicott divides the national guilt the same way, idolatry strictly and a heathenish manner of worshipping Jehovah under the form of a bullock; he takes the literal sense of the disputed verb as covered and defends the very reading his colleagues reject, that Hebrew verbs of covering and hiding are often used of dealing treacherously, noting that this form occurs nowhere else. He calls the pillars and Asheras sacred trunks, contrasts the solitary watchtowers with the embattled cities, and renders the idols the dunglings, a term of contempt.

Gill says the sin enlarged on through the whole discourse is idolatry, and allows two accounts of the secrecy, either that they were ashamed to commit such things openly or that they covered them with plausible pretences. He observes that groves of trees could not be set under green trees, so that idols of stone and wood must be meant, and remarks that the Indians still place idols in little groves or at the foot of a shadowing hill; on the last verse he takes the word for dunghill gods and notes that Sterculius was a name of Saturn, given him for finding out how to make land fruitful with dung.

Clarke says the idolatry was universal, from the largest city to the smallest village and from the public watchtower to the shepherd's cot, and identifies the groves with the rites of Ashtaroth. Wesley gives the same two accounts of the secrecy as Gill, that they were ashamed of what they did or covered the worship of the calves with fair pretences, and reaches the spread of the high places from the other side, that they were set up even in the most uninhabited parts.

Henry notices what the historian passes over, the weakness of Israel and the strength of Assyria, since the Assyrian was but the rod of his anger, and refuses to let the ruin be called a bare act of sovereignty rather than necessary justice. He lists three gifts that bound them, their liberty, their law with God himself for king, and their land emptied of nations whose casting out was itself a warning; he observes that only the idolatry is specified though they had broken all the second table, reads the secrecy as evidence of their atheism, and says that having forsaken the one place God chose they knew no end of high places.

13.pericope_label: Yet the Lord testified against Israel, and against Judah, by all the prophets, and by all the seers, saying, Turn ye from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and my statutes, according to all the law which I commanded your fathers, and which I sent to you by my servants the prophets. Notwithstanding they would not hear, but hardened their necks, like to the neck of their fathers, that did not believe in the Lord their God. And they rejected his statutes, and his covenant that he made with their fathers, and his testimonies which he testified against them; and they followed vanity, and became vain, and went after the heathen that were round about them, concerning whom the Lord had charged them, that they should not do like them. And they left all the commandments of the Lord their God, and made them molten images, even two calves, and made a grove, and worshipped all the host of heaven, and served Baal. And they caused their sons and their daughters to pass through the fire, and used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the Lord, to provoke him to anger.

schools.summary: Ellicott would render the verb adjured rather than testified against, a solemn charge rather than an accusation, reads the Hebrew as by the hand of all his prophets, every seer, and distinguishes the seers as men outside the prophetic order who came forward on a sudden divine impulse. He prefers to read the closing clause according to all that I sent to you by my servants the prophets, since the prophets interpreted the law rather than bringing it; he notes that neck is singular and that the Greek and Syriac read more than the neck of their fathers, insists the unbelief charged is moral rather than intellectual, and gives the word vanity its root sense of a breath. On the Asherah he quotes Schlottmann at length for a real trunk planted in the ground, rootless but not branchless, standing for nature beside Baal the lord of the world. Keil and Delitzsch say the historian names Judah in order to indicate beforehand that Judah was preparing the same fate for itself, take the following of vanity as a judgment on the whole aim of their life, and observe that worship of the host of heaven is charged nowhere else against the ten tribes and appears first in Judah under Manasseh.

Gill supplies the names of the prophets who testified, Ahijah the Shilonite, Elijah and Elisha, Hosea, Amos and Micah, locates the covenant rejected at Sinai and Horeb, takes Baal and Moloch for one and the fire-rite as done either by way of lustration or so as to burn, and draws the legal conclusion that he who offends in one point is guilty of all.

Clarke says the succession of prophets is what leaves the conduct inexcusable, since they preached not only repentance but God's readiness to forgive on return, and glosses the selling of themselves as abandoning themselves to work all iniquity with greediness. Wesley describes the seers by what they received, men to whom God declared his mind by revelations and visions, makes the hardened neck a metaphor from stubborn oxen that will not bow to the yoke, says the idols are called vanity for their nothingness and that by long worship of them the people were made like them, and names the host of heaven plainly as the stars.

18.pericope_label: Therefore the Lord was very angry with Israel, and removed them out of his sight: there was none left but the tribe of Judah only. Also Judah kept not the commandments of the Lord their God, but walked in the statutes of Israel which they made. And the Lord rejected all the seed of Israel, and afflicted them, and delivered them into the hand of spoilers, until he had cast them out of his sight. For he rent Israel from the house of David; and they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat king: and Jeroboam drave Israel from following the Lord, and made them sin a great sin. For the children of Israel walked in all the sins of Jeroboam which he did; they departed not from them; Until the Lord removed Israel out of his sight, as he had said by all his servants the prophets. So was Israel carried away out of their own land to Assyria unto this day.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the tribe to mean the kingdom and reads removed them out of his sight as founded on the old local conceptions of deity, makes Judah no real or permanent exception to either the sin or the penalty, names Ahaziah and Ahaz as the kings who favoured the northern worship, and holds that Israel is used in the narrow sense in these verses, the spoilers being the Syrians and the Assyrians. On the rending he answers that the Hebrew as it stands can only mean Israel rent, there being no object after the transitive verb, and prefers to restore the passive with the Vulgate, Israel rent himself away; he finds in that verse the source of the whole evil, separation from Judah leading to the calf worship and that to idolatry outright, and observes at the close that the land was not wholly emptied though the distinctive character of the nation was lost. Keil and Delitzsch take all the seed of Israel for the whole nation rather than the ten tribes, and separate rejection, which consisted in chastisement and delivery to plunderers, from the thrusting out of his face, which is exile; they hold Jehovah to be the subject of the rending, since the ellipsis otherwise required is too harsh and it is God who is said elsewhere to have rent the kingdom from Solomon, and they enter a caution that the phrase unto this day proves nothing either way about a later return.

Gill says Judah was drawn into the idolatry of the ten tribes by their example and persisted in it after seeing what befell them, puts the rejection in the prophets' terms, that a Lo-ammi was written on them and a bill of divorce given, and keeps the rending with the Lord as done according to his purpose and his prophecy.

Clarke reckons under the name of Judah all of Benjamin and Levi with those Israelites who abandoned their idolatries and joined themselves to Judah, and counts what the banishment cost, the promised land, the temple and every ordinance of righteousness at once. Wesley makes the same count of who was left, the greater part of Benjamin with those of Simeon and Levi incorporated, holds that the rejection of all Israel does not extend to every individual since many removed into Judah, and lays the making of Jeroboam king on a people who would not wait until God had invested him.

The Lord, according to his purpose and decree and agreeably to his prophecy

24.pericope_label: And the king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel: and they possessed Samaria, and dwelt in the cities thereof. And so it was at the beginning of their dwelling there, that they feared not the Lord: therefore the Lord sent lions among them, which slew some of them. Wherefore they spake to the king of Assyria, saying, The nations which thou hast removed, and placed in the cities of Samaria, know not the manner of the God of the land: therefore he hath sent lions among them, and, behold, they slay them, because they know not the manner of the God of the land. Then the king of Assyria commanded, saying, Carry thither one of the priests whom ye brought from thence; and let them go and dwell there, and let him teach them the manner of the God of the land. Then one of the priests whom they had carried away from Samaria came and dwelt in Beth–el, and taught them how they should fear the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott names Sargon as the resettling king, quoting his annals for the settlement of conquered Babylonians in Syria and of Arab tribes in Samerina, in the very phrase the verse uses, and makes Esarhaddon only a later reinforcement; he identifies the towns from the inscriptions, Kutie with its temple of Nergal found at Tell-Ibrahim and the two Sipars named for the sun and for Anunit, gives the natural cause of the lions and observes that the sacred writer endorses the reading the colonists put on them, would render men spake for they spake, takes the manner of the God of the land as his appointed worship, and notes that the priest was teaching, a permanent work, in Bethel because he was a priest of the calves. Keil and Delitzsch argue the king cannot be Shalmaneser, since a considerable period intervened between the deportation and the resettlement, and take it for Esarhaddon on the evidence of Ezra; they too give the natural multiplication of the lions in a wasted land and note that the author looked on them as sent in punishment according to Leviticus.

Gill allows Shalmaneser but inclines to Esarhaddon, and on the priest sent back reports that an Arabic writer calls him Uzziah and Epiphanius Esdras, concluding he was doubtless one of the priests of the calves, since no others had been carried away and since he chose to dwell at Bethel where he had probably officiated before.

Clarke explains the policy rather than the king, that one people is removed entire and another substituted so that the newcomers have no patrimony worth contending for; he derives Cuthah from Cush and notes that the Samaritans were therefore called Cuthaeans, says wild beasts would necessarily increase in an emptied land without any supernatural intervention while allowing that God likely did send them as a scourge, and alone looks forward, that imperfect as the teaching was it ended by overthrowing their idolatry. Wesley adds that the neglect of the God of the land was strange even by heathen standards, since men commonly worshipped the gods of the country they came into, and infers the character of the priest's teaching from the manner of making priests that followed.

Henry stands back from the detail, that never was land lost for want of an heir and that it is sad for the holy land to become heathen again; he presses the hand of God in the lions, sent as a rough welcome to check their insolence and to teach them that though they had conquered Israel the God of Israel had power enough to deal with them, observes that Assyrians begged to be taught what Israelites hated to be taught, and says a prophet would have done them more good, since this man might teach them to do better but was not likely to teach them to do well.

29.pericope_label: Howbeit every nation made gods of their own, and put them in the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made, every nation in their cities wherein they dwelt. And the men of Babylon made Succoth–benoth, and the men of Cuth made Nergal, and the men of Hamath made Ashima, And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim. So they feared the Lord, and made unto themselves of the lowest of them priests of the high places, which sacrificed for them in the houses of the high places. They feared the Lord, and served their own gods, after the manner of the nations whom they carried away from thence.

schools.summary: Ellicott would begin the passage with a plain and rather than howbeit and says the colonists did not fear Jehovah in any monotheistic sense but added his worship to that of their ancestral gods; he thinks the spelling of Succoth-benoth has suffered in transmission and identifies the goddess Zarpanitum, the seed-maker, consort of Merodach, points for Nergal to the colossal lions that guarded Assyrian doorways and to a syllabary naming him god of Kutha, says nothing is known of Ashima and rejects the identification with the Phoenician Eshmun, declines to identify Nibhaz and Tartak at all though the forms have an Assyrio-Babylonian cast, reads Adrammelech and Anammelech as Adar is prince and Anu is prince, and renders of the lowest of them as of all orders or promiscuously, finding in that a further sign that the worship of Jeroboam was being restored. Keil and Delitzsch report the rabbinic figures of the dog and the ass but prefer the view that makes both infernal powers, and argue from the burning of children that Adrammelech and Anammelech were related to Moloch, offering glorious king from the Semitic and fire-king from the Persian.

Gill takes Succoth-benoth as the booths of the daughters and refers it to the prostitution at the temple of the Babylonian Venus, reporting besides the rabbinic hen and chickens and a guess at the Pleiades; he gives Nibhaz the shape of a dog from a root meaning to bark and Tartak that of an ass, but adds a wholly different derivation, that Nibhaz means the remote one seeth and so the sun while Tartak is a chain and may denote the fixed stars chained in their places. He notes that the newcomers set their images in the high places Israel had built, and sums the result in four words, that they worshipped both.

Clarke says the gods they made were copies of what they had worshipped at home, derives the name Venus itself from benoth, offers the solar orb with a cock for emblem as Nergal and fire as Ashima, identifies Nibhaz with the barking Anubis and describes a stone image of the kind lying before him as he wrote, and takes Adrammelech for the sun and Anammelech for the moon or the Moloch of the Ammonites; on the priesthood he takes of the lowest of them at face value, since the office was neither respectable nor lucrative. Wesley observes that the sacrificing taught must have been to the true God, since for their own gods they needed no instruction and would have allowed no outsider to minister.

34.pericope_label: Unto this day they do after the former manners: they fear not the Lord, neither do they after their statutes, or after their ordinances, or after the law and commandment which the Lord commanded the children of Jacob, whom he named Israel; With whom the Lord had made a covenant, and charged them, saying, Ye shall not fear other gods, nor bow yourselves to them, nor serve them, nor sacrifice to them: But the Lord, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt with great power and a stretched out arm, him shall ye fear, and him shall ye worship, and to him shall ye do sacrifice. And the statutes, and the ordinances, and the law, and the commandment, which he wrote for you, ye shall observe to do for evermore; and ye shall not fear other gods. And the covenant that I have made with you ye shall not forget; neither shall ye fear other gods. But the Lord your God ye shall fear; and he shall deliver you out of the hand of all your enemies. Howbeit they did not hearken, but they did after their former manner. So these nations feared the Lord, and served their graven images, both their children, and their children’s children: as did their fathers, so do they unto this day.

schools.summary: Ellicott holds that the writer has in view the remnant of the ten tribes who amalgamated with the new settlers, and later names the subject plainly as the Ephraimites, clinging to the long established worship of the calves; he resolves the paradox of fearing and not fearing by degree, that they did not fear him in the sense of a right fear nor honour him as the law prescribes, and notes that the Greek drops both negatives. He observes that the prohibition of fearing other gods is repeated three times as the main point of the covenant, marks the pronoun in the promise of deliverance as emphatic, and dates the closing notice by counting two generations from the captivity of Ephraim to the exile of Judah and the age of the last editor of these books. Keil and Delitzsch confine the former customs to the usages introduced when the new inhabitants settled, divide the next verse between the ten tribes who did not hearken and the Israelites left in the land who continued in the old manner, and say only that the mixed worship lasted until the books of the Kings were written.

Gill leaves three readings of the closing verdict open without choosing between them, the colonists keeping their own former customs, or keeping those of the idolatrous Israelites, or the captives themselves unreformed by their troubles; he locates the covenant at Sinai, observes that the first table chiefly concerns the worship of the one true God, and closes where the chapter began, that these nations did what Israel had done before them, serving the Lord and their images together as Israel had served God and the calves.

Clarke argues from the notice that the chapter must have been written before the Babylonish captivity, since after it none of the Israelites ever lapsed into idolatry, and allows that it may chiefly describe the heathen settled among the remains of the ten tribes; on the central verse he distinguishes three things, the object of worship, the reason for it in a deliverance of irresistible power, and the manner of it in reverence, humility and sacrifice, in which a man confesses that he has sinned and deserves the death the victim dies. Wesley says that whatever they pretended they worshipped their own calves and inventions, that God will not accept a mongrel worship, that the proof lies in a life lived in constant breach of the statutes, and that the name Israel is named here as an aggravation; he stretches the closing notice furthest, above three hundred years to the time of Alexander the Great.

debates.question: Who are the they that do after the former manners?

positions.position: The remnant of the ten tribes amalgamated with the settlers, the Ephraimites clinging to the calf worship
The colonists, whose usages are the ones just described, the not hearkening belonging to the ten tribes
Any of three, the colonists, the captives, or those left in the land

debates.question: How far does unto this day reach?

positions.position: Not past the Babylonish captivity, after which no Israelite lapsed into idolatry
Two generations past the fall of Samaria, to the exile of Judah and the last editor of these books
To the time when the books of the Kings were written
Above three hundred years, to the time of Alexander the Great

outliers.claim: Takes the central verse of the covenant apart into the object of worship, the reasons for it and the manner of it, finding the manner in three verbs: reverence, the bowing of the knee, and sacrifice

themes: Unto this day they do after the former manners: they fear not the Lord, neither do they after their statutes, or after their ordinances, or after the law and commandment which the Lord commanded the children of Jacob, whom he named Israel;
With whom the Lord had made a covenant, and charged them, saying, Ye shall not fear other gods, nor bow yourselves to them, nor serve them, nor sacrifice to them:
But the Lord, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt with great power and a stretched out arm, him shall ye fear, and him shall ye worship, and to him shall ye do sacrifice.
And the statutes, and the ordinances, and the law, and the commandment, which he wrote for you, ye shall observe to do for evermore; and ye shall not fear other gods.
And the covenant that I have made with you ye shall not forget; neither shall ye fear other gods.
But the Lord your God ye shall fear; and he shall deliver you out of the hand of all your enemies.
Howbeit they did not hearken, but they did after their former manner.
So these nations feared the Lord, and served their graven images, both their children, and their children’s children: as did their fathers, so do they unto this day.
